name: dumplings
instructions:
From Anita Spring Councel, Southern Roots — drop dumplings for chicken-and-dumplings / stew tops.

INGREDIENTS:
- 2 cups all-purpose flour
- 2 tsp baking powder
- 1/2 tsp salt
- 2 tbsp unsalted butter (cold)
- 1 egg
- 3/4 cup milk

PROCEDURE:

1. MIX THE DRY: whisk together flour, baking powder, and salt in a bowl.

2. CUT IN THE COLD BUTTER: cut cold butter into the dry mix (fingers, pastry cutter, or two knives) until the mixture looks like coarse meal with pea-sized butter bits.

3. WHISK THE WET: in a separate small bowl, whisk together the egg and milk.

4. COMBINE: pour the wet into the dry and stir JUST until a sticky dough forms. Don't overmix.

5. DROP INTO BROTH: drop spoonfuls of the dough onto the surface of a simmering soup or stew. Cover the pot and simmer for about 15 minutes — DON'T lift the lid early. The dumplings should puff up and be cooked through.
notes:
Source: Anita Spring Councel, Southern Roots. Drop dumplings for chicken-and-dumplings / stew tops.

=== BISCUIT-STYLE DUMPLINGS — RICHER THAN WATER+FLOUR ===

Baking-powder, butter, and milk (plus egg per Council) version — the southern-american chicken-and-dumplings style. Fluffy, biscuity, with their own flavor. Distinct from the simple water+flour dumplings the french chicken soup notes mention as the inline default; this version is an upgrade when you want the dumplings to be a more flavorful component in their own right rather than just a neutral starch carrier.

=== EGG IN COUNCIL'S VERSION (VS EGGLESS TRADITIONAL) ===

Council's recipe adds 1 egg to the dough — richer and slightly more structured than eggless biscuit-dumpling recipes. Some traditional versions skip the egg. Keeping it here per source; the added richness fits chicken-and-dumplings' comfort-food register.

=== COLD BUTTER MATTERS ===

The butter should be cold when cut in — same logic as biscuit / pie-crust technique. Cold butter pockets create steam during cooking, which is what makes the dumpling fluffy rather than dense. Room-temperature butter melts into the flour and gives you a flat, cakey result.

=== DON'T LIFT THE LID ===

Covered simmering is non-negotiable. The steam trapped under the lid is what cooks the tops of the dumplings. Lifting the lid early releases the steam and gives you raw-on-top dumplings.

=== DON'T OVERMIX ===

Stir just until the dough comes together. Gluten development from overmixing yields tough, chewy dumplings instead of tender biscuity ones.

=== FITS FRENCH CHICKEN SOUP ===

Works as the carb component in french-chicken-soup if you want richer dumplings than the inline water+flour version. The biscuity flavor doesn't fight the white-wine-and-tarragon broth — if anything, the butter-milk-egg character complements it.

=== CHANGES FROM PRIOR CAPTURED VERSION ===

Earlier version in this file used 1 cup flour + 1 tsp sugar + 1/2 cup milk + no egg. Council's version: 2 cups flour (double), NO sugar, 3/4 cup milk (up), 1 egg (new). Better attribution, more traditional-southern (no sugar in the dumpling itself).
